Cited prior papers are not separately extracted. No supplementary document is identified in this article.

annotations.text: Blood samples were collected immediately before the meal (t = 0 min) and at 30, 60, and 120 min after the start of the meal.
Intervals were measured in minutes from the start of the meal.
P values were calculated using the Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test.
Blood glucose is reported in mg/dL.
Serum insulin is reported in μIU/mL.
Glucose iAUC is reported in mg/dL × min.
Insulin iAUC is reported in μIU/mL × min.

Transcription was checked against the rendered table. The PDF text layer substitutes 6 for ±, 2 for some minus signs, and m for the insulin micro-unit symbol. CSV strings preserve the visible numerical precision, thousands separators, and composite cells.

tables.notes: Complete 14-row table. The text reports a 36.7% glucose decrease at 60 minutes whereas this table prints −37.0%; text reports glucose iAUC0–120 as 2,001 and 73% lower whereas this table prints 2,001.5 and −73.5%. The separate prose reports are preserved in their comparison records. No values have been recomputed to reconcile these differences.

result_groups.title: Meal order and postprandial glucose and insulin responses
result_groups.question: Does consuming vegetables and protein before carbohydrate change glucose and insulin responses to the same meal in adults with type 2 diabetes?
result_groups.investigation: One within-subject crossover pilot investigation of 11 metformin-treated overweight/obese adults, with two meal-order visits one week apart.
result_groups.grouping_reason: All 14 local comparisons concern the same meal-order question within one experiment. Outcomes, measurement times, integration windows, and baseline comparisons are variations within that investigation; the single table is provenance, not the grouping criterion.
result_groups.summary: Carbohydrate-last meals had lower glucose at 30, 60, and 120 minutes and lower glucose iAUC, with lower insulin at 60 and 120 minutes and lower insulin iAUC over 0–60 and 0–120 minutes. Table 1 also reports baseline comparisons and the 30-minute insulin and 0–30-minute insulin iAUC comparisons. All are retained regardless of statistical significance.

context.population: Metformin-treated overweight/obese adults with type 2 diabetes
context.comparison: Protein and vegetables before carbohydrate versus carbohydrate before protein and vegetables
context.study_design: Within-subject crossover pilot; carbohydrate-first at visit 1 and carbohydrate-last at visit 2
author_interpretations: The authors describe the glucose effect as comparable to that of pharmacological agents preferentially targeting postprandial glucose; this paper does not contain a direct drug comparison.
Reduced insulin excursions are interpreted as suggesting improved insulin sensitivity; insulin sensitivity is not directly measured in this study.
The authors suggest that timing carbohydrate ingestion during a meal may improve glycemia.
limitations: Responses were analyzed only up to 120 minutes after meal ingestion.
The authors call for longer follow-up to assess delayed effects and underlying mechanisms.

source_disclosures.funding: Clinical and Translational Science Center at Weill Cornell Medical College (UL1TR000457), and the Dr. Robert C. and Veronica Atkins Curriculum in Metabolic Disease at Weill Cornell Medical College Grant.
source_disclosures.conflicts_of_interest: No potential conflicts of interest relevant to this article were reported.

source_snippets.locator: e98, middle column, discussion
source_snippets.text: In this pilot study, we demonstrated that the temporal sequence of carbohydrate ingestion during a meal has a significant impact on postprandial glucose and insulin excursions.

source_snippets.locator: e98, middle column bottom to right column top, interpretation
source_snippets.text: The magnitude of the effect of food order on glucose levels is comparable to that observed with pharmacological agents that preferentially target postprandial glucose. Moreover, the reduced insulin excursions observed in this experimental setting suggest that this meal pattern may improve insulin sensitivity.

source_snippets.locator: e98, right column, limitation and future work
source_snippets.text: A limitation of the study is that we analyzed glucose and insulin responses up to 120 min following meal ingestion, as this study was designed to test postprandial glucose levels as practically measured by patients with type 2 diabetes. Further studies with longer follow-up to delineate the full impact, including delayed effects and the mechanisms underlying the glycemic effect of food order, are indicated.

source_snippets.locator: e98, right column, concluding paragraph
source_snippets.text: this pilot study suggests that improvement in glycemia may be achieved by optimal timing of carbohydrate ingestion during a meal.

result_groups.notes: The 14 local records are not 14 independent studies. They share 11 participants and one intervention protocol. Source uncertainty is SEM for outcome means and SD for participant descriptors. Prose/table numerical differences are retained in the affected records.

source_snippets.locator: e98, left column bottom through middle column, meal protocol
source_snippets.text: After a 12-h overnight fast, subjects consumed an isocaloric meal (628 kcal: 55 g protein, 68 g carbohydrate, and 16 g fat) with the same composition on 2 separate days, 1 week apart. During the first visit, the food order was carbohydrate (ciabatta bread and orange juice), followed 15 min later by protein (skinless grilled chicken breast) and vegetables (lettuce and tomato salad with low-fat Italian vinaigrette and steamed broccoli with butter); the food order was reversed a week later.
